clinicalPearls: A biochemical finding of persistently raised plasma methionine without accompanying homocystinuria, rather than a single disease
The commonest inherited cause is methionine adenosyltransferase I/III (MAT1A) deficiency, which is usually benign
Other genetic causes include glycine N-methyltransferase deficiency, and the treatable methylation defects S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase and adenosine kinase deficiency
Secondary hypermethioninaemia occurs with liver disease, prematurity, high methionine or protein intake, and tyrosinaemia type 1
The key clinical distinction is separating the benign causes from the serious, treatable ones
A boiled-cabbage or sulphurous breath odour from dimethyl sulfide may accompany markedly raised methionine
Classical homocystinuria from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency also raises methionine but is defined by the associated homocystinuria
Diagnostic approach uses plasma amino acids, total homocysteine, S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine, liver function and targeted genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Methionine sits at the head of the transmethylation pathway, being activated to S-adenosylmethionine before serving as the universal methyl donor and then entering the transsulfuration and remethylation cycles. Plasma methionine rises whenever its onward metabolism is impeded or its supply is excessive. Reduced conversion to S-adenosylmethionine, as in MAT I/III deficiency, or a block further along the methylation cycle, as in AHCY, GNMT or adenosine kinase deficiency, causes methionine to accumulate; secondary elevations reflect impaired hepatic handling or high intake. The clinical significance therefore depends entirely on the underlying mechanism, ranging from a harmless finding to a marker of treatable neurological or hepatic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Hepatic dysfunction, prematurity, high-protein intake or tyrosinaemia type 1
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids to confirm isolated methionine elevation
Plasma total homocysteine to exclude classical homocystinuria and remethylation defects
S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine to differentiate methylation-cycle disorders
Liver function tests to identify hepatic causes
Succinylacetone or relevant testing to exclude tyrosinaemia type 1
Targeted gene sequencing (for example MAT1A, GNMT, AHCY, ADK) guided by the metabolite pattern
redFlags: Neurological signs, developmental delay or regression suggesting a treatable methylation defect
Hepatic dysfunction or coagulopathy pointing to AHCY, adenosine kinase deficiency or liver disease
Raised homocysteine indicating homocystinuria rather than isolated hypermethioninaemia
Very high sustained methionine warranting prompt clarification of the cause
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; isolated MAT I/III or GNMT deficiency is generally benign, whereas AHCY and adenosine kinase deficiency and untreated secondary causes carry more serious implications that improve with appropriate treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming all isolated hypermethioninaemia is benign and missing AHCY or adenosine kinase deficiency
Failing to measure homocysteine and so overlooking classical homocystinuria
Not checking S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine, which are needed to separate the genetic causes
Attributing the finding to diet or liver disease without excluding an inborn error
Over-restricting methionine in a benign case, risking essential amino acid deficiency
references: Mudd SH. Hypermethioninemias of genetic and non-genetic origin
Blau N. Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Identify and treat the underlying cause, since management depends entirely on the specific mechanism
Institute a methionine-restricted diet where a treatable methylation defect such as S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase or adenosine kinase deficiency is confirmed
Generally observe without specific treatment in benign MAT I/III or GNMT deficiency, considering modest methionine reduction only when levels are very high with a risk of demyelination
Treat secondary causes such as tyrosinaemia type 1 and hepatic dysfunction on their own merits
Distinguish benign from serious causes using total homocysteine, S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine together with targeted genetic testing
Monitor plasma methionine and neurological status and adjust dietary methionine accordingly
Offer genetic counselling for the inherited recessive causes and manage through a metabolic service
